title_en: Vibecoding Teen Behind Nuked GTA 6 PC Port Project 'Leonida' Vows to Continue, Says Parents 'Have Warned Me About What Could Happen'
summary_en: The 15-year-old vibecoder behind a GTA 6 PC port project Take-Two recently shut down has vowed to continue their work despite the potential for further action from the company.
body_en:
The 15-year-old vibecoder behind a GTA 6 PC port project Take-Two recently shut down has vowed to continue their work despite the potential for further action from the company.
‘NotRexed’ is behind ‘Project Leonida,’ which was at one point leading the race to create a PC port of GTA 6 following the recent leak of an Xbox build. Cyberleek, the infamous leaker behind many early GTA 6 gameplay clips, reportedly released the Xbox build of GTA 6 last week, and vibecoders have been attempting to port the game to PC since.
Fueled by AI, progress has been swift, with clips showing GTA 6 running on PC at a higher frame rate than on console, and one video even showing basic multiplayer. Obviously, Rockstar Games, which will no doubt release GTA 6 on PC officially at some point, and parent company Take-Two will be watching the homebrew scene’s every move like a hawk.
In the case of Project Leonida, Take-Two has already taken action. NotRexed was organizing and sharing work on a Discord group, and hosting their findings on a GitHub repository, when cease and desists from Take-Two hauled everything offline. NotRexed then took to social media to announce they'd decided to call it a day.
“I quit guys. I’m sorry,” NotRexed said. “I really want to make cool stuff but every single time s**t happens that I can’t control so I’m stepping away. Thank you everybody, especially in the Discord that allowed me to have this opportunity.”
NotRexed went on to insist that they were finding it tough to run Project Leonida while also going to school. “Rockstar taking my server down was only part of the reason. Like I’ve said before, I’m a 15-year-old kid,” they said. “Managing school and sports is hard enough without having middle aged men yell and complain to you on Discord. Goodbye.”
However, NotRexed has now returned, and promised to continue the project. “Ignore my other posts,” NotRexed said after changing their mind. “Something’s coming soon. Leonida is NOT dead. I have been doing a lot of work behind the scenes. I’ll have some stuff to show all of you soon.”
IGN spoke to NotRexed to find out why they’re doing this, whether they understand the risks, what they’ll do if they get in legal trouble, and what their parents think of it all.
“It’s just a hobby of mine,” NotRexed said in a private message. “I started doing similar things with porting games to the web back in the start of 2026, and I’ve always just thought of it to be cool.”
Before generative AI, NotRexed had no interest in porting games to other platforms, they said. But after finding out it was possible in 2025, they’re now taking on one of the most powerful publishers in video games. Interestingly, there’s no real motive behind it.
“I’ve always been interested in tech and mess around with it a lot,” they said. According to them, even their parents are aware of what they do and are largely supportive of it. “Yes, they know about all my projects and work I do, and they’re pretty encouraging about it,” they claimed.
It made me wonder if they were fully aware of the legal risks involved in such an undertaking. “Yea, they have warned me about what could happen,” NotRexed insisted when I asked if their parents knew about the potential legal issues. “I’m still continuing my work as of now tho because even tho T2 took down my repo and Discord they have never sent an email or message directly to me. If I do get into legal trouble I’m probably gonna stop working on it but possibly have a friend continue it.”
How feasible is this? IGN asked Matt Freedman, a veteran game developer with expertise in both traditional development and the controversial emerging technology of AI.
“A recompilation is different from a port,” Freedman said. “But yes, an AI driven recompilation of GTA 6 is very doable and wouldn't have the same 'game feel' problems that an AI-driven port would have.”
He went on to explain the differences between decompilations, recompilations, and ports. A decomp is where someone manually reverse engineers a game to run on other systems, like the Mario 64 PC port. “This is very time consuming and requires a human to do the work and effectively 'guess' how the game works,” he said.
A port takes existing assets or creates new ones and essentially builds a new version of the same game to work on another system. The Witcher 3’s Switch port is an example of this. “A team took The Witcher 3 code base and assets and then modified them by hand to work on the Switch,” he said.
For recomps, people use large language models (LLMs) to break down a game and rebuild it, essentially reverse engineering the title for whatever system the user wants. “Since LLMs natively can read binary, they're able to understand the specific code better than humans can,” Freedman explained.
A decomp or port of GTA 6 would not be easy — not least because Rockstar uses proprietary tech, including its in-house Rage engine, to power its games. “When it comes to AI, it'll depend on how well it has previously seen the engine or the low level SDK,” Freedman replied when asked about this complication. “A well studied proprietary engine with lots of public information would be easier for it to understand. A custom engine for an obscure CPU would be much more difficult for it.
“So, something like Rockstar's Rage engine would be more difficult for it to figure out than something like a game made in Unreal. But… given that a 15-year-old was able to have an AI port GTA 6 to PC, it's clearly not the biggest lift out there.”
All the while, Take-Two is working to take down various homebrew community efforts from GitHub, as the race to release an unofficial GTA 6 PC port appears close to the finish line. There’s even a website tracking the various attempts to recompile, emulate, or port the leaked Xbox Series build to PC.
The big question for Take-Two is, can it do anything meaningful to stop a working, playable build of GTA 6 on PC from getting into people's hands? GitHub takedowns can only go so far, as the homebrew scene uses AI to speed along development. It's a question IGN recently asked when people started to work on a PC port of Nintendo Switch 2 exclusive, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake .
Take-Two stands to make billions of dollars more from the official PC release of GTA 6, so any unofficial version is a significant business risk. In a recent interview with IGN sister site RPS , former Rockstar North technical director Obbe Vermeij said that Rockstar may be keen to port GTA 6 to PC as soon as possible , due to the explosion of AI-generated clones and ports.
Earlier this month, Strauss Zelnick, the boss of Take-Two, responded to the threat of AI-assisted reverse-engineering and decompilation of games in an interview with IGN. He said he was taking the issue seriously, and insisted that fans will prefer to play GTA 6 officially, as Rockstar intended, over an unofficial PC version.
Here’s the exchange:
IGN: We've seen hackers using AI to clone games much faster than ever before, even try to jailbreak consoles. And there is some concern about this leading to potentially GTA 6 being made available on PC unofficially or places that you aren't releasing it. I was just wondering how much of a threat this is to your business? And, is there anything meaningful you can do about it?
Strauss Zelnick: I don't think it’s a financial matter, in terms of a threat to our business. I do think it’s a creative matter. It's important to everyone, our developers and our consumers alike, to deliver the experience Rockstar envisions. And at the same time, of course, we protect our intellectual property vigilantly. So we are focused on these concerns. We're not in the least cavalier about them. Technology is advancing quickly. And at the same time, I do think that pretty much everyone wants the Rockstar experience as Rockstar intended.
IGN: Related, last week Anthropic confirmed they took steps to block Claude from reverse engineering video games. I would assume you would welcome that. And would you like to see other AI companies like OpenAI do the same thing to prevent people from using these powerful AI models to clone your games?
Strauss Zelnick: I think all companies should be protecting intellectual property, their own and everyone else's. And if you're in the intellectual property business, which Anthropic is and OpenAI is, then it seems ironic on the one hand to stomp on someone else's IP and hope that yours is protected.
During an investor-focused Q&A following the release of Take-Two’s latest financial report, attended by IGN, Zelnick was asked multiple times about the AI reverse-engineering problem. He, again, had strong words in response, suggesting Take-Two was ready to lawyer up.
“This business has been largely immune to piracy concerns forever because of file sizes, complexity of piracy, being connected to servers and the like,” he began. “And undoubtedly, it would be very difficult to replicate the experience of consuming our game as intended because of technical limitations.
“That said, it's going to become more of a challenge, as you said, and we're aware of that. So we are utterly focused on enhancing our technical defenses and enhancing our legal activities appropriately. And at the same time, without in any way being cavalier, every entertainment business that exists is subject to some element of piracy. So this is likely to invade our business to a greater or lesser extent. I think it will be manageable and we are focused on it.”
Kirk McKeand is a Contributor on IGN News. Find him on Twitter @MckKirk
